Pele Yoetz 317:5: And the man who is a Jew and believes in the Torah and in the words of our sages, of blessed memory, that God will bring into judgment every regard for his own soul and for his Maker's honor, should heed the words of the wise, flee from transgression, and do good in every possible way, so that he delight in abundance for his soul. And every good thing requires strengthening and overcoming one's inclination day by day, and one who comes to purify himself is assisted from Heaven (Shabbat 104a).
Pele Yoetz 318:1: Kevi'ut Tzedakah (Fixed Charity) — One who fixes a set amount to give to some poor person, monthly or weekly, has in this matter both something praiseworthy and something to criticize. To its credit, the poor man's life does not hang in doubt, wondering from where his help will come, and his heart is steadfast, trusting in the regular giver, having something to rely upon — and this is a great benefit for the poor man. But on the other hand there is something to criticize, for sometimes it happens that the giver's hand is diminished and he cannot give, yet what he gives is out of embarrassment, and the poor man thereby enters into a category resembling robbery. And furthermore, sometimes this poor person does not need it so much, and had the giver been free to choose, he would have given to a more fitting and worthy place, or to his own impoverished relatives; but what can he do, since the poor man does not let him discontinue his allotment, and sometimes his teeth grind and he is consumed, according to the times and according to what kind of person he is, and he cannot do anything. Behold, therefore, it is good for a man to hold to this: to give some poor person a fixed allotment he can rely upon, doing so with a small amount so that it not wither, and beyond this let him not withhold his hand from giving to every one who asks, according to what kind of person he is and according to the blessing of the Name given to him at that time. “Good is the man who conducts his affairs with justice” (Psalms 112:5), and both together are good.
Pele Yoetz 319:1: Kerovim (Relatives) — It is known, the statement of our sages, of blessed memory, on the verse (Exodus 22:24), “The poor person with you”: your own poor and the poor of your city — your own poor come first (Bava Metzia 71a). And it is written (Isaiah 58:7), “And do not hide yourself from your own flesh.” And it is written (Proverbs 17:17), “And a brother is born for adversity.” And we have established (Yoreh De'ah, sec. 251, para. 8) that one who has wealthy relatives is not given from the charity fund, since it is incumbent on his relatives to support him. And how much more so if his father and brothers are poor, that he is obligated to have mercy on them and support them according to his ability, with honor and a cheerful countenance, for if he gives much to others and leaves his father and brothers cast in hunger, he is destined to give an account, and in place of charity it shall be counted as an outcry against him — unless his brothers are unworthy, in which case it is permissible [to withhold]. But regarding his father and mother there is no room for exemption, and it is an obligation incumbent upon him to fulfill “Honor your father and your mother” (Exodus 20:12; Deuteronomy 5:16). What is this honor? Feeding him, giving him drink, clothing him, and providing him shoes (Kiddushin 31b), and especially in their old age he is obligated to sustain their gray hair and provide sufficiently for their needs with great honor and a cheerful countenance. And even if a man gave all the wealth of his house, he could not repay what his father and mother suffered for him in their bodies and their money.
Pele Yoetz 319:2: And it is true that it is hard for a father and mother to be dependent on their children, and people have already said: if a father supports ten sons, the father laughs and the sons laugh, but if ten sons support a father, the father weeps and the sons weep. But an obligation is incumbent on the son to appease him with good words, for this is the essence of the commandment of honoring father and mother, as our sages, of blessed memory, said (ibid. 31[a]): there is one who feeds his father fattened fowl yet inherits Gehinnom, and there is one who grinds at the millstone for his father yet inherits the Garden of Eden — as in the incident recorded in Midrash Rabbah.
Pele Yoetz 319:3: And an obligation is incumbent on every man to draw his relatives close, as our sages, of blessed memory, said (Yevamot 62b), and to rejoice in their joy and grieve in their trouble and to go in and out of their house. And King Solomon, peace be upon him, already said (Proverbs 19:7), “All the brothers of a poor man hate him,” while “many are the friends of the rich” (ibid. 14:20). And such is the custom of the world: if he has any relation, even a distant one, to a wealthy man, he fills his mouth boasting and takes pride in it, saying, “So-and-so is my relative”; but if he is a poor and needy man, he is ashamed to say that he is his relative, either because of the honor that he feels is beneath his dignity, or because he fears the expense on his behalf will increase, and therefore he pretends not to know of his kinship, and relatives become strangers.
Pele Yoetz 319:4: And the especially upright man ought to draw his poor relatives close, visit them, bring them to his house, honor them and support them, and call them by the name of “relative,” for through this he gladdens the heart of the wretched and revives the heart of the downtrodden, and it shall be counted as a great commandment, for they are among the broken vessels of the Holy One, blessed be He. And if he distances them, they complain about their bad fortune and are crushed, and the Name shall contend their cause, Heaven forbid [for having caused this].
Pele Yoetz 319:5: But he must not go out of line for the sake of his relatives, nor prettify falsehood for them, nor help them in falsehood, for the wise man said: “Although you are our beloved, truth is more beloved.” And according to right reasoning, it is not fitting for a person to help his brothers and relatives in their dispute with others, even regarding a matter of truth, lest the listener suspect him of flattering his relatives. And he must also be concerned lest, because of his kinship, he fails to see fault in his relative; therefore let him remain silent and not enter into the dispute, and not take sides with either party. And how much more so if he sees and understands that his relative acted improperly, that it is fitting for him to be the first to strike him on the head, so that truth not be lost, and that it be accepted and welcomed, since it is heard from the mouth of his relative, and all the people shall come and declare his righteousness, for pure and upright is his deed, that he shows no favoritism — “who said of his father and mother, I have not seen him, and did not recognize his brothers, and knew not his own children” — for the sake of the Name.
Pele Yoetz 320:1: Kenas (Fine) — An obligation is incumbent upon those who sit on seats of judgment and the leaders of communities to fine sinners according to the sin and according to the person, whether in money or in disgrace. But a scale and balances of justice are needed, to weigh with a holy shekel, neither adding nor subtracting, so that no mishap or dispute result. “And a soft tongue breaks a bone” (Proverbs 25:15), so let him speak not in terms of a fine, but in terms of the rectification of the soul and in terms of atonement, for this is indeed the truth: when there is no judgment below, there is judgment above, and all the people shall hear and fear, and the merit of the many depends on him.
Pele Yoetz 320:2: And the great fence, so that people believe his deeds are for the sake of Heaven, is that the wise man who imposes the fine derive no personal benefit from that fine. And they already explained that this is the intent of the statement of our sages, of blessed memory, who said (Yoma 22b): “Any Torah scholar who does not avenge and bear a grudge like a snake is not a Torah scholar” — they were precise in saying “like a snake,” which bites but derives no benefit; so too he should derive no benefit. And through this the wise man is recognized as one who fears the Name and trusts in the Name, that he show no favor to the poor and give no honor to the great and fear no man, for judgment belongs to God, and the Lord loves justice, and those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing (Psalms 34:11).
Pele Yoetz 320:3: And how good and what a great fence it is, to fulfill every good thing and withdraw one's hand from every sin, that he accept upon himself to give a fine if he transgresses, so that he shall certainly not transgress and shall be holy.
Pele Yoetz 321:1: Kevurah (Burial) — Our sages, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 8a), regarding this every pious person shall pray to You at a time of finding — this refers to burial, for there are several who do not merit burial and become food for dogs, wild beasts, birds of the sky, and fish of the sea. And there are those buried in disgrace, may the Merciful One save us, and there are those who die on the first day of a festival and are buried by gentiles, and there are those who die on Friday at twilight and lie two nights without burial and the like — and all this is among the wonders of the One perfect in knowledge, who disciplines a person with various forms of suffering to atone for his sins, for his own good. Go and learn from Rabbi Chatzpit the interpreter, whose mouth brought forth pearls, yet in the end his tongue was dragged in the garbage by the mouth of a dog (Kiddushin 39b). And many perfect and righteous men lay as dung upon the face of the earth, as it is written (Psalms 79:2), “They have given the corpses of Your servants as food to the birds of the sky, the flesh of Your pious ones to the beasts of the earth. They have poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem, with none to bury them.” Behold, therefore, whoever this has happened to regarding his deceased, this shall be his comfort: that the Lord intended it for his good. And therefore it is fitting to seek the Name's favor — just as a person prays for all his needs, so let him pray for this too. And I have already said that at the conclusion of every prayer and every supplication, it is fitting to conclude and say: “And whatever is good in Your eyes for Your service and for satisfaction before Your glorious throne and for the rectification of our soul, spirit, and higher soul, do with us.”
Pele Yoetz 321:2: And it is fitting to seek mercy that one's burial be in the Land of Israel, and that his burial take place on the day of his death, for it is a great satisfaction to the deceased that his corpse not lie overnight, and however much they hasten his burial, they grant him satisfaction and rest for his soul. And this shall be the kindness performed by the burial society, that they strive to hasten the burial with all their effort.
Pele Yoetz 321:3: And how good is the portion and how pleasant is the lot of a person if he merits that his passing and burial occur on Friday afternoon, after midday, and in the Land of Israel, for they wrote that he is saved from the judgment of the beating of the grave. And it all depends on a person's deeds, but prayer bears fruit, for our God is merciful and hears prayers and supplications, and therefore let him pour out his speech over everything. And a person is pitiable whose rest depends on the decay of his body, and therefore man's hope is the worm, that it consume him well an hour sooner, for as long as his body endures, his flesh pains him and his soul mourns over him. Therefore it is good for a man to be buried in good earth that dissolves the body quickly, and it should be firm ground and not moist, for then the decomposition of the body is delayed. And therefore some instruct that lime be placed beneath and upon their bodies so that the body dissolve quickly. And some have written that this is not proper, for it appears as though outwitting His judgments, blessed be He, and none can save from His hand, and if he is liable to be disciplined, nothing prevents the Name from disciplining him with harsher and more bitter sufferings. But in the holy Zohar it is said that as long as the body endures there is prosecution against it, and when the body is consumed the prosecution ceases, and it is known that the Holy One, blessed be He, desires kindness, only that the prosecution delays it. Behold, therefore, it is evidently proper to do this (and I command that this be done for myself as well). And the best thing is to do good deeds and guard against every evil, and to repent with complete repentance, and to withdraw one's hand from eating meat and drinking wine and other pleasures and vanities of this world — perhaps he shall merit to be saved from deceit and from the beating of the grave, and his flesh shall dwell securely.
Pele Yoetz 321:4: And included among the needs of burial and rest for the deceased is that a tombstone be placed on his grave immediately after the seven days of mourning have passed, for the deceased has seven spirits, and on each day of the seven days of mourning one spirit enters the grave, and one must, immediately after the seven days pass, on the eighth day, seal the grave with a tombstone so that spirits not enter and lodge there. And if he cannot place the tombstone immediately, in any case he should hasten as much as he can and not leave the deceased without a tombstone. And it is likewise very beneficial for the deceased to separate from him all kinds of spirits and afflictions of humans, that they perform for him, near the burial, the order of circuits as arranged in the books — that is, that ten men circle the deceased seven times while reciting seven times the verse “And let the pleasantness [of the Lord be upon us]” (Psalms 90:17), and each time recite one of the seven verses corresponding to the forty-two-letter Name, and from there immediately bring him into the grave. These things are true kindness, and whoever does them, just as he causes rest, so shall his own soul rest, and his reward is with him and his recompense before him.
Pele Yoetz 322:1: Korbanot (Sacrifices) — Many statements of our sages, of blessed memory, are known, who said (Vayikra Rabbah, ch. 7) that the reading of the sacrifices is exceedingly valuable before the Omnipresent, and it is accounted to them as though the Temple had been built in their days and as though they had offered all the sacrifices. And likewise in the holy Zohar they elaborated greatly on the praise that comes to one who studies the order of the sacrifices and the order of the compounding of the incense, to the point that they said: if the world knew how exalted is the act of the incense before the Holy One, blessed be He, they would take every word of it and place it as a crown upon their heads like a crown of gold, and if he intends it properly every day, he has a good portion in this world and the World to Come, and death shall be removed from him and from the world, and he shall be saved from all the judgments of the world and from the judgment of Gehinnom. And they further said regarding the matter of the sacrifices, that a covenant has been made, that those angels who mention guilt to bring evil upon it cannot do it anything but good, and all of them shall recall it for good. And at a time when a plague occurs among mankind, it has already been decreed, and a proclamation passes through all the host of heaven that if his children on earth enter synagogues and study houses and recite with the desire of their soul, dwelling upon the matter of the incense with its spices, the plague shall be annulled from them. The eye sees the great benefit of studying the sacrifices and the order of compounding the incense.
Pele Yoetz 322:2: And happy are the Israelites, all of whom study the portion of the sacrifices and the order of compounding the incense and the order of the arrangement and the chapter “Which is their place,” and there are those who read all the portions of the sacrifices; but this is the difficulty, that the language of the holy Zohar is precise and says, “and let him intend them and set his heart and desire upon them.” It appears that one who reads without intention of heart shall not attain the benefits mentioned in the holy Zohar. And it is fitting and proper to strengthen oneself to study the order of the sacrifices and the order of compounding the incense with intention and desire of the heart, to give satisfaction to our Creator, who repays good reward to those who do His will.
Pele Yoetz 322:3: And the man whom the Name has graced to have his portion among those who sit in the study house — how good and pleasant it is that he fix times to study in the Talmud or in Maimonides in the laws of the sacrificial service, for this gives greater satisfaction to his Creator than other studies. Regarding such a thing it is said (Berachot 17a), “Happy is he whose toil is in Torah and who gives satisfaction to his Creator.”
Pele Yoetz 323:1: Keriat Shema — The Shema is an important commandment that includes accepting the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven and the yoke of the commandments, and the intention of the heart is what matters, for if he did not direct his heart at least in the first verse, he has not fulfilled his obligation (Orach Chaim, sec. 60, para. 5), for he must intend that he accepts upon himself the blessed Name as Lord and Patron, and that he believes the blessed Name is One and unifying, one in heaven and on earth and in the four directions of the world, and that he is ready to give his life for the sanctification of the Name. And it is a pity that some, alas, do not even intend this much, and it turns out that they die without having fulfilled the commandment of the Shema. Whoever hears this, let him take it to heart to intend this from now on, and he shall repent and be healed. And it is best to have intention throughout the entire Shema, for ideally intention is required throughout its entirety.
Pele Yoetz 323:2: And the kabbalists wrote that according to the intention one has in the Shema, so shall he be able to have intention in prayer. And this is the intent of the statement of our sages, of blessed memory (Berachot 5a): whoever recites the Shema, harmful spirits stay away from him. The essential harmful spirits are those that cause harm to a person and confuse his mind during his prayer, and when he recites the Shema properly, those harmful spirits stay away from him.
Pele Yoetz 323:3: And our master ruled in the Shulchan Aruch (Orach Chaim, sec. 61, para. 1): let him recite the Shema with awe, fear, trembling, and quaking. And how does one come to this quality? By visualizing as though standing before a King exalted and lofty, awesome and fearsome, a mighty King, the Holy One, blessed be He, who says to him, “And you shall love the Lord your God,” etc., until the end of the Shema, and through this his heart shall be filled with love of the Name, thinking: what are we and what is our life, man being like a mere breath, yet our Creator chose us — after whom did the King of the world go out, wishing that he love Him? Is there in the world such great good and such great virtue as this? And this is what I understand to be the meaning of “And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might” — and if you say, for what shall we love Him, what good has He done for us beforehand? To this he says: if it were only this — that these words which I command you exist, that I, an exalted King, desire that you love Me — when you place this upon your heart, it is enough, for you have no greater good than this. And likewise when it says (Deuteronomy 11:16), “Guard yourselves lest your heart be seduced,” etc., let him visualize the like. And let the man tremble and shrink, for I have already said that for every transgression committed, whether in thought, speech, or deed, it is included in “and you shall serve other gods” (ibid. 17), for it turns out that he serves his own inclination and sets aside his Creator's will to do his inclination's will.
Pele Yoetz 323:4: And it is known that regarding the evening Shema, which we pray before the stars come out, what fulfills the obligation is the Shema recited on the bed, and one must be very careful about it and not fail to recite it — he should not lie down until he has recited it, for many times a person lies down to rest a little and says, “I shall not sleep, now I shall rise and recite it,” and sleep overtakes him and he remains without having recited the Shema, losing much good. For they said that whoever does not recite the Shema, or recites it after its time has passed, is liable to excommunication, may the Merciful One save us.
Pele Yoetz 323:5: And regarding this too one must take heed, for many who are lazy and love to sleep during the summer months, and especially on Shabbatot and festivals and joyous occasions, mostly let the time for reciting the Shema pass. And the man who fears the Name should recite it early in the morning, and say: “Behold, I am reciting the Shema to fulfill through it my obligation, that which our Creator commanded us; if its time passes before I recite it with the congregation at ‘Yotzer,’ [this recitation counts as my obligation], and if its time does not pass, let my reading now be like reading from the Torah alone.” And one must be very precise with its letters, and this can only be done through great deliberation, care, and long habituation. And it is fitting to strengthen oneself to give satisfaction to our Creator, for they said (Berachot 15b) that whoever is precise with its letters, they cool Gehinnom for him. And this is a great benefit for one who knows a little of what Gehinnom is.
Pele Yoetz 323:6: And when he recites it in his house, or when he recites the Shema on his bed, he must be careful that there be no handbreadth of his wife exposed from a place usually covered, and likewise a woman's hair is nakedness, even regarding his own wife, for the Shema, and closing his eyes does not suffice, but he must turn his face to another side. And he must likewise be careful that the place be clean of all filth. These are some of the ways of one who wishes to accept upon himself the complete yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven.
Pele Yoetz 324:1: Kol (Voice) — “The voice is the voice of Jacob” (Genesis 27:22), and great is the merit of the voice of Torah, which ascends and pierces the heavens, and it is exceedingly valuable before the Omnipresent that one who reads aloud with clear speech gladdens God. And how greatly have those who study while mumbling erred, or those who study a book with their voice unheard, losing much good. This is comparable to one who could earn a thousand gold coins and settles for five hundred. And if what he loses affected only himself, we would remain silent, but this is the difficulty: that he fails to give satisfaction to his Creator and causes harm to himself, for he forgets his learning, as our sages, of blessed memory, said. And our sages, of blessed memory, said in the Talmud (Eruvin 54a): open your mouth [when] reading Scripture, open your mouth [when] repeating [oral teachings], so that it be retained by you and that you lengthen your life, as it is written (Proverbs 4:22), “For they are life to those who find them, in the mouth,” and it is written (II Samuel 23:5), “Ordered in all things and secure” — if it is ordered in the 248 limbs, it is secure.
Pele Yoetz 325:1: Keri (Nocturnal Emission) — The books of ethics are already full of discussions in bitter language about the sin against the covenant and the severity of the sin of nocturnal emission and the wasteful discharge of seed. And the books explain the rectification for this sin and matters beneficial for guarding against it — go and see in the holy book Reshit Chokhmah, and the book Seder HaYom, and the book Tziporen Shamir, and the book Shnei Luchot HaBrit, and many others. And it has already been printed also in the order Yosef LeChok in the Torah portions of Shovavim [the winter Torah readings]. Whoever is God-fearing and tender-hearted, over whose head the raging waters have passed — the sins of youth — let him remember his Creator in the days of his youth and rectify his transgression with all his ability before the days of evil come, and in whatever he does he shall not be at peace [with himself]. And his sin shall always be before him, and he shall be despicable and loathsome in his own eyes, for truly, even if a man lived a thousand years and did repentance during them, he could not fulfill his obligation according to the severity involved and according to the smallness of our worth and the limitation of our acts of repentance — except that the Holy One, blessed be He, does not act tyrannically with His creatures, and His right hand is extended to receive those who return with a whole heart and do all that is in their power to do. Only let his inclination not easily persuade him to say that he cannot do it and mortify his body, but rather let the righteous man examine — perhaps he can, for the Name shall be among his helpers, for He gives strength to the weary and increases might to those who have no strength.
Pele Yoetz 325:2: But let him always remain in doubt, lest the little that came before him he did not rectify his distortion. And all his days, remembering the sin of his youth, his flesh shall pain him and his soul shall mourn over him. And happy is the man who fears the Name from his youth and is saved from this sin — how good is his portion and how pleasant is his lot; he can easily acquire the entire order of holiness, and all his days shall be at ease and his flesh shall dwell securely. For one over whose head this sin has passed shall live a life of pain all his days, if he merits to be learned and know the severity involved; but one who has merited to be saved from it, happy is he in this world and it is well with him in the World to Come. But who is truly clean in these generations? Even if he does not commit every aspect of this prohibition, he commits some of them, for even if he is saved from adultery, homosexual relations, and manually discharging seed wastefully, he is not saved from evil thoughts through forbidden sights and comes to nocturnal emission in his dreams. And greater than this, regarding his own wife they said (Nedarim 20b) that if he does not sanctify his thought and directs his mind toward another woman during relations, he is considered like an adulterer and his children from his wife are like mamzerim. And if he does not delay upon her until the sparks are exhausted [i.e., ensures her satisfaction], he is considered like one who discharges seed wastefully. And if the woman is not careful regarding her menstrual status and the manner of her purification, that it be according to law and halachah, then he lies with an impure woman and blemishes the covenant. Whoever desires life should have regard for his own soul and for his Maker's honor, and hasten his own escape and rectify his distortion, and make a fence and a barrier and a guard for his guard, so that he not again return to folly — perhaps his tranquility shall be prolonged, and he shall find the means of his redemption and ransom his soul.
Pele Yoetz 326:1: The letter Resh: Rachamanut (Compassion) — Compassion is one of three signs that Israel possesses: they are doers of kindness, bashful, and compassionate. And our sages, of blessed memory, already said (Shabbat 151b): whoever has compassion on creatures shall have compassion shown to him from Heaven, as it is said (Deuteronomy 13:18), “And He shall give you compassion, and have compassion on you, and multiply you.” And a person must possess this from knowledge of his Maker, of whom it is written (Psalms 145:9), “And His mercies are upon all His works.” He has compassion even on the dog and delays its meal within its bowels, and gives the animal its food and to the young ravens who cry out, and His mercies have grown so great that He gives long patience to transgressors of His will and benefits them even when they anger Him, and this and more He has compassion on His creatures beyond measure, to a place our own hands cannot reach, in such a way that the mouth cannot describe the greatness of His mercies, kindnesses, and compassion, and we must walk in His ways. And it is known that the suffering of animals is a Torah prohibition. And it is written in Sefer Chasidim (section 669) that those who feed a horse excessively in order to run it before them, not for any need of life but merely for pleasure riding, of them it is said (Proverbs 12:10), “And the compassion of the wicked is cruelty.”
Pele Yoetz 326:2: And it is known what is told in the Talmud (Bava Metzia 85a), that Rabbi's sufferings came through an incident and departed through an incident. They came through an incident: a certain calf was being brought to be slaughtered, and it went and hid its head under Rabbi's cloak. He said to it, “Go, for this you were created.” They said, “Since he showed no compassion, let sufferings come upon him” (it seems that this calf contained some reincarnated soul and knew it was going to be slaughtered, and it was hard for it to bear the pain of slaughter while in the body of the animal, and it sought from Rabbi that he seek mercy for it, to leave the animal before slaughter, and he said to it, “Go, for this you were created” — within the animal, to suffer this pain, and this is your rectification — and since he did not have mercy to seek mercy for it as it requested, they did not have mercy on him — consider this).
Pele Yoetz 326:3: And if we are honest, it seems one must be concerned regarding every animal, beast, and fowl, not to say in front of it, “Go slaughter this animal or this fowl,” but rather as some say, “Go place a chain around its neck.” And they departed through an incident: once his maidservant was sweeping the house and found some baby weasels; she wanted to kill them. He said to her, “Leave them be, for ‘His mercies are upon all His works’ is written.” They said, “Since he shows mercy, let mercy be shown to him.”
Pele Yoetz 326:4: And it is stated in the holy Zohar that even a snake, a person is not obligated to kill it — see there the full language. And this has already been elaborated at length in the pamphlets of Orot Eilim — see there. And certainly this is a matter of piety, for in the Talmud it appears that it is permissible to kill it even on Shabbat (Shabbat 121b), but he should hold to the beneficial half: as for striking dogs, cats, and the like for having done him some harm even unwittingly, and because this is their livelihood [natural behavior], there is even a prohibition involved. And how much more so and how much more certainly is it fitting to have compassion on creatures created in the image of God — our brothers, the children of Israel, all of whom are children of one man, like one man, like one body. And even a man who has done him evil and treated him improperly — let the Name repay him according to his deed, and let him not take revenge nor bear a grudge, but rather have compassion on him and help him in whatever comes from his hand, and by the measure with which a person measures, he is measured (Megillah 12b; Sotah 8b).
Pele Yoetz 326:5: However, regarding the trait of compassion, a scale and balances of justice are needed, to weigh with a holy shekel, for in a place where there are two parties, and to have compassion on one requires being harsh toward the other, which straight path should a person choose? The straight and good path according to the Torah and according to what is upright — for example, if a borrower and a lender come before you: if he sees that the borrower has the ability to pay in cash or in movable property, or even from his expensive clothing and household items, silver, gold, jewels, and the like, and does not wish to pay, it is fitting to be harsh toward the borrower and have compassion on the lender, and to compel the borrower through gentile courts and through bans and by every means possible, until he pays his debt. But if they see that the borrower conducts himself in good faith and strives and makes efforts to pay his debt little by little, and there is hope that he can pay his debt through business dealings little by little, and if they force him to pay everything at once he would break or lose his credit, it is fitting to have compassion on him and gain him time by having him pledge collateral, or a guarantor, or an oath that he will pay his debt by the time set for him. And one must always be compassionate toward the oppressed and harsh toward the oppressor, and save the oppressed from the hand of his oppressor.
Pele Yoetz 326:6: And one must be harsh toward transgressors of the Torah and break their fangs, for it is good to have compassion on his Maker's honor and raise up the banner of the Torah. And likewise let him be harsh, like a raven, toward his sons and household members [regarding transgression], and toward his own body, to mortify it, for it is good to have compassion on his soul and on the Creator of his soul. And likewise let him be harsh toward himself, to break his desires and withdraw his hand from every evil thing and fulfill every good thing, for it is good to have regard for himself, that he delight in abundance for his soul and not be judged with evil judgments, for many are the pains of the wicked. And the essence is to have regard for the honor of the Holy One, blessed be He, that the Name rejoice in His works, those who do His will. (And behold, love is included in compassion — see what I have written above under the entry “Ahavah,” with the help of Heaven.)
Pele Yoetz 327:1: Reiyah (Sight) — Sight is severe, for it leads to transgression, since the eye sees and the heart desires, and how many severe and grave evils come through the eyes. If one gazes at forbidden women and the heart desires and comes to transgression or to thoughts of transgression, great is his sin. And even if he does not come to transgression at all, nor gazed at her except to recognize her, the very act of gazing is itself a transgression and blemishes the eyes of his soul and the supernal eyes. And one who gazes at a rainbow or at the moon commits a transgression thereby. And they said in the Talmud (Chagigah 16a) that this is included among those who have no regard for their Maker's honor, of whom it would have been better had they not come into the world. And one who gazes at the face of a wicked person commits a prohibition and blemishes his eyes, and how much more so at the faces of gentiles or at idols, for he transgresses what is written (Leviticus 19:4), “Do not turn to idols.” And the definition of a wicked person is such that they said (see Choshen Mishpat, sec. 17, in the name of Sefer Chasidim) that one should not gaze at the faces of litigants, since they said (Avot 1:8), “When they stand before you, regard them as wicked.” And likewise in the holy Zohar they said that it is forbidden to gaze at the face of an angry person while he is angry. And through sight a person robs, extorts, steals, and kills, and almost all transgressions are not committed without the sight of the eyes.
Pele Yoetz 327:2: And even a sight that involves no transgression at all, such as gazing at the vanities of this world, drags along transgression, for it frees his heart for idleness and confuses his thought, and he cannot direct his mind to fear and love the Name and cling to Him, and to have proper intention in his prayers and blessings without the admixture of strange thoughts and evil musings — whether because it is natural in man and it is impossible not to see something or some creature, man or woman, from man to beast to every created thing, without any thought occurring to him at the moment of his sight; and sometimes the thought becomes mixed and continues from matter to matter and from subject to subject, until the man is astonished and thinks, “From where did these thoughts come to me?” and he looks back to understand the end of the matter from its beginning, and meanwhile his tongue, like a messenger, completes its mission and finishes his prayer and blessing, with nothing at all remaining in his possession — who caused him this, from the beginning of the thought? The sight.
Pele Yoetz 327:3: And also, when a person blemishes the eyes of his soul, he cannot see intellectual matters, and his sins separate between him and his Father in Heaven, and he cannot direct his mind. And it is stated in the holy Zohar that it is forbidden to gaze at anything that would bring a person to joy in this time, for the smoke of the burning of the Holy Temple is placed between the eyes, and Scripture says (Psalms 101:5), “Haughty eyes I cannot bear.” And especially in prayer, if he does not close his eyes or place them within the book, his punishment is great, for the Angel of Death shall come to him early and he shall not see the face of the Divine Presence at his passing. And according to the evil of the eyes, it would have been fitting to desire and pray to be blind, or to blind them with one's own hands, were it not that the good of the eyes is also great and they are needed greatly for the service of the blessed Name. And therefore the Holy One, blessed be He, made eyelids for the eyes, so that he could close and open them at will.
Pele Yoetz 327:4: And a person must strengthen himself with great might and effort to shut his eyes from seeing evil. And he should not gaze at women, nor at beast or fowl at the time they are mating, and at any strange or forbidden sights. And happy is he who can fulfill what the early ones used to do, not to gaze beyond four cubits — of him it is said (Job 22:29), “And the lowly of eyes He shall save.” For by removing his eyes from material things, this shall remind him to think of intellectual and spiritual matters, and to fear and love the Name and cling to Him. And this is the intent of what we say, “For the eyes of all wait upon You.” And the kabbalists further wrote that in the eye there is the Name “Havayah,” and when he gazes at the earth, which is “Adnut” [sovereignty, associated with the Name Adonai], it turns out to be a unification. But if he gazes outward at what is unnecessary, it turns out to be a separation. And they further wrote that one who guards his sight guards his seed, and one who blemishes it certainly blemishes the seed, for the seed is the light of a person's eyes. And just as every good thing requires strengthening, how much more so the guarding of the eyes, which run swiftly, whose loss is great and whose evil and punishment are abundant, and one who is careful with them, in guarding them, has great reward. And they said in the Midrash (Yalkut Shimoni, Proverbs, remez 425) that whoever guards himself and shuts his eyes from seeing evil, the Holy One, blessed be He, says, “That is My judgment.”
Pele Yoetz 327:5: And for what he has transgressed and sinned with his eyes, if he wishes to rectify it, streams of water shall flow from his eyes, as it is written (Psalms 119:136), “Streams of water flow down my eyes because they [others] have not kept Your Torah” — meaning, because the eyes of Your Torah have not been guarded. And let him also drive sleep from his eyes and rise at midnight, or at least let his eyes anticipate the watches, and let him be among the servants of the Lord who stand in the house of the Lord by night — such as in places where they hold study sessions and study together every Friday night and on the night of Shavuot and the night of Hoshana Rabbah — this is a great rectification, to strengthen oneself to stand on guard, driving sleep away, not slumbering nor sleeping the entire night, even under great pressure and grief, provided that he can manage not to sleep during his prayer, for this is a great rectification for the blemish of sight. And likewise, if he has committed bundles of transgressions with his eyes, let him perform corresponding bundles of commandments with them, such as gazing at tzitzit, and let his eyes behold a book to read Torah, prayers, and blessings. And it is good to gaze at the face of one's teacher, which is beneficial for wisdom, as it is written (Isaiah 30:20), “And your eyes shall see your teachers.”
Pele Yoetz 327:6: And just as gazing at the face of a wicked person causes harm, correspondingly, gazing at the face of a righteous, good, and wise person causes good and draws a flow of holiness upon his soul. And it is stated in the Talmud (Eruvin 13b) that Rabbi said: “The reason I am superior to my colleagues is that I saw Rabbi Meir from behind; had I seen him from the front, I would have been even more superior.” And they further said (Yerushalmi Eruvin 5:1) that one who receives the face of his teacher is as one who receives the face of the Divine Presence. And they further said (Chagigah 5b): it is written (Psalms 49:10), “And shall he live forever and not see the pit?” for he shall see the wise die. If one who sees the wise even in their death is thus rewarded, how much more so in their lifetime. And there is also a rectification for the blemish of sight: to weep over a worthy person and over one's own sins, and over the destruction of the Holy Temple, streams of water flowing from his eyes, and through this he shall merit to behold the pleasantness of the Lord and visit in His sanctuary.
Pele Yoetz 328:1: Redifah (Pursuit) — It is written (Proverbs 21:21), “Whoever pursues charity and kindness finds life.” The matter of “pursuing” means that it flees from him and he pursues it — that is, for example, there is a person who has nothing and does not wish to take charity, and he suffers and is distressed; one must pursue him to give him charity without his knowledge, such as selling to him cheaply, or placing coins in front of him where he passes so that he find them as though by chance, or placing money in his purse without his knowledge, or giving his wife household necessities, or to those who buy household necessities for him — and other such methods and strategies he should employ in order to benefit him. And with such a man lies the essence of charity, and regarding such a thing it is said (Psalms 41:2), “Happy is he who considers the poor.”
Pele Yoetz 328:2: And likewise what is said (Psalms 34:15), “Seek peace and pursue it,” means: if peace flees from him — such as when his adversary is a harsh man who stirs up disputes and does not desire peace, in the manner of what is written (ibid. 120:7), “I am peace, but when I speak, they are for war” — even so, let him pursue peace, for peace is great. And likewise what is written (ibid. 23:6), “Surely goodness and kindness shall pursue me,” meaning that it is fitting for a person to flee from the good things of this world, either because it is dangerous, being liable to lead one out of line, as it is written (Deuteronomy 8:12), “Lest you eat and be satisfied,” etc., “and your heart grow haughty and you forget the Lord your God” — and as King Solomon, peace be upon him, said (Proverbs 30:8-9), “Give me neither poverty nor riches, lest I be full and deny, and say, ‘Who is the Lord?’” And also because the good things of this world are deducted from a person's share of the good things of the World to Come, and one hour of tranquility of spirit in the World to Come is better [than all the life of this world].
